short_summary: Meta has been ordered by a New Mexico court to pay a $25 billion penalty following a state trial over data privacy practices and the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

sources.name: CNBC
sources.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case

sources.name: TechCrunch
sources.title: Meta ordered to pay $25B in case related to Cambridge Analytica scandal

paragraphs: Meta has been ordered by a New Mexico court to pay a staggering $25 billion penalty in a landmark data privacy case stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal nearly a decade ago. According to court filings, the massive financial sanction follows a jury trial in Santa Fe where the social media giant was found liable for misleading state residents regarding how their user data was collected, safeguarded, and protected from harmful content.

The jury concluded that the company committed more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act. Although each transgression carried a civil penalty as high as $5,000, New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew determined the final fine. The judge pointed to the extraordinary number of willful violations, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, and the systematic nature of the misstatements as factors supporting the maximum level allowed under the law. Furthermore, the court ruled that interest on the penalty will accrue at an annual rate of 15% until it is paid in full.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez praised the outcome during a press conference, emphasizing that powerful technology companies are not beyond the reach of the law and that such violations carry real consequences. Torrez remarked that the state might have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years with the funds. The state pursued the litigation independently after choosing not to join an overarching multi-state settlement that resolved similar data privacy claims elsewhere.

Meta strongly criticized the decision. C.J. Mahoney, the company's chief legal officer, released a statement arguing that the ruling and the attorney general's enforcement approach make conducting business in the state nearly impossible. Mahoney asserted that the lawsuit attempts to impose a tax on speech and enforce new rules for online communication, adding that the company is fully confident it will prevail on appeal.

This legal blow adds to a long history of financial fallout from the Cambridge Analytica controversy, which originally erupted in 2018 under the leadership of Mark Zuckerberg. The scandal rocked the firm when it was revealed that a political consulting firm improperly accessed the information of 87 million users. Judge Mathew noted in the filing that Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation it promised, citing pressure from senior executives to keep costs down and a desire to avoid creating precedent for future investigations. While Meta previously resolved numerous class-action lawsuits and federal settlements regarding data privacy, child safety, and mental health, the New Mexico case has resulted in by far the largest single penalty the company has faced to date.

facts.fact: A New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion penalty in a data privacy case stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
A jury in Santa Fe found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, misleading citizens about user data safeguards.
New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew set the penalty, noting interest will accrue at 15% annually until paid.
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the ruling, stating the company is confident it will prevail on appeal.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez oversaw the trial after the state did not join a separate nationwide settlement.
